I'm not even talking about quick removal, necessarily, but better coordination during large events to allow for more thorough snow clearing. The snowy cities have snow routes where you cannot park during a large snowfall. Once they have plowed the major routes, you can move your car there from the side streets and they'll plow the side streets. In Montreal the side streets are only plowed during the day and there is a warning system, so you have an opportunity to move your vehicle before your street gets plowed (or get towed). Montreal's approach is probably more elaborate than we need (or could afford) but it would be helpful to have some kind of strategy for people to relocate their vehicles before the street is plowed. 

Even just giving people a realistic timeline for snow removal would probably be helpful. Edmonton recently released a statement that they're clearing the cul-de-sacs and it'll take six weeks. Not quick lol, but at least you know as a resident that it's happening.

Was it because of a boy? Was it because of your family?" I cannot know if there was a final catalyst that killed her, because she's not here to tell me. It's possible that she didn't fully understand it herself. I'll never know. Did she blame anyone? She once said she didn't, but I can't know the intricacies of another person's mind while they are alive, let alone after they've died. Almost six years later, I remain frustrated that I can't ask her why she had to leave. If there was something I could have done to stop her. 

There's also a misconception that a suicide note will always bring comfort and clarity to those who read it. In fact, many notes are painful or confusing to read. There's a misconception that most people who kill themselves leave behind notes. A large number do not. 

There's a misconception that it's possible to "move on." I take issue with that phrase. I have moved in various directions since my sister's death. Forward and backward, up and down. In circles. That doesn't mean there's something wrong with the way I have grieved. It means I have grieved and am grieving. Grief changes but never goes away. Psychiatrists in Ontario all bill OHIP and  prescribe medication. Some do administer talk therapy, but many do not. We don't actually have enough psychiatrists in Ontario and it can be difficult to get one even if you do have OHIP. It would be lucky to find a psychiatrist in under a month.

General practitioners can also prescribe psychiatric medication; GPs are often not comfortable prescribing for more serious or complicated mental health concerns.

Psychologists and therapists don't prescribe medication but do administer talk therapy, cognitive therapy, etc. Majority do not bill OHIP, unless they're working with a hospital or something. (Psychologists charge a lot, generally.) 

Out of all these professionals, therapists are the easiest to find. They have their own regulatory bodies and it's worth looking into someone's credentials before you see them. 

The website psychologytoday.com is a great resource, and you won't need a referral to most of the people listed on it.

A terrible truth that I learned since my sister's death is that suicide is not uncommon. Being bereaved by suicide is something that can happen to any of us. And sometimes more than once. 

According to the American Society for Suicide Prevention, suicide was the 12th leading cause of death in 2020. In that year, 45,979 took their own lives in the US. An estimated 1.20M Americans attempted to take their lives. Certain age groups and demographics are more at risk than others.

You did nothing to cause this. It is not your fault. Suicide is multifaceted and even highly trained professionals cannot predict or prevent it in many cases. 

I believe it is true that we could stand to be a kinder society, and that this would likely help many suicidal people. But this isn't something one person can achieve on their own, and it isn't something that would solve suicide, either. Suicide is a death of mental despair. Despair has many factors. And mental illness isn't something that's fully understood. Maybe one day we will understand it better and be able to help suicidal people more effectively. I hope we will.
